title: Avoid the Drama and the People Who Live for It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article names and dissects a familiar workplace type: the team member who is drawn to conflict because it satisfies a need for attention and significance. It describes how such people manufacture or exaggerate controversy, play victim or aggressor in disputes, and drain a team's energy in the process. The prescribed leadership response is deliberate withdrawal of attention — listening without feeding the theatrics, declining to legitimize exaggerated claims, and asking for de-escalation. The piece ends with an unusually blunt line: leaders who can't curb the pattern should be prepared to point the person toward the door.
points: People drawn to drama are described as having a deep need for attention, which drives them to manufacture or exaggerate conflict where none needs to exist.
The recommended leadership response is to withhold attention — listen, nod, and decline to escalate rather than getting pulled into the manufactured conflict.
Leaders who engage the theatrics as if they were legitimate end up spreading the negative emotional cost across the entire team.
If a team member refuses to curb drama-seeking behavior after being starved of attention, the piece recommends removal from the team as the final step.
quotes: Being in the center of drama makes them feel important and alive.
They exaggerate the negative in any situation. Worse yet, when drama doesn’t exist, they create it.
Allowing them to suck you into their theatrical world is the mistake every good leader makes until they recognize the pattern.
They starve these negative thespians of attention and ask them to take the temperature down regarding any issue, perceived or real.
Good leaders don’t give legitimacy to anything that is false, exaggerated, or dysfunctional.
